text: M. Caillaux lengthily conferred with the Rt. Hon. Montagu Norman, Governor of the Bank of England, before seeing Winston Churchill at noon.

label: text
text: The principal question discussed by M. Caillaux and Mr. Norman was the French commercial debt, namely, the engagements of the French Government to repay annually sums advanced by the Bank of England to the Bank of France.

label: text
text: It is understood that M. Caillaux will see Mr. Reginald McKenna in the afternoon.

label: text
text: That the present Anglo-French negotiations did not end in definite agreement, but he would return to Paris with new proposals which are to be submitted to the consideration of his colleagues, was the only concrete statement made by Mr Caillaux in the evening, discussing with pressmen to-day's numerous meetings.

Swarmpcott, August 25.
President Coolidge now thinks the American Debt Funding Commission should listen to outstanding debtor nations' pleas for more lenient treatment than accorded to Britain and determine in what measure the request should be granted.

label: text
text: The President is of the opinion that the Funding Commission, when working out the British arrangement, established a principle afterwards approved by Congress as the basis of settlement. Every debtor must be of the ability to pay on this basis, not varied in any instance by the Versailles or any other treaty or agreement.

text: M. Caillaux spent the morning at the French Embassy with his experts. M. Caillaux later visited financiers in the city, meeting Mr. Churchill at the Treasury late in the afternoon.

label: text
text: While M. Caillaux was busy at the French Embassy Mr. Churchill was similarly engaged with his experts at the Treasury studying the French viewpoint. Owing to last minute changes in the plans M. Caillaux went to the Treasury at noon to see Mr. Churchill.

text: While expressing satisfaction at the “particularly cordial atmosphere” in the conversations between Mr. Churchill. and M. text: Canton, if its attitude can properly be gathered from a whirlwind sort, of pronouncement in the "Canton Gazette," is very angry with the people of Hongkong because of the public meeting they recently held about affairs in China, observas the "North China Daily News." A few weeks have passed since the Hongkong meeting was held, but the "Gazette" only got news of it on August 4 through Chinese papers, because communications are "father bad." Whose fault, we think the "Gazette" ought to explain, for it is certainly not that of the British. To get on with the main business, however. The "Gazette," says that although the resolutions may not be quite accurately translated the spirit must leave be in fully preserved, for anybody familiar with the characteristics of the Britishers in the colonies will easily recognize the spirit permeating their attitude towards the people, to presido over whose destinies they consider themselves as having been specially ordained by Providence itself. The writer shows in this sentence, deplorable lack of originality, and in fact, all through, his stuff is not nearly so good as what we have read拥manating from Canton in the past. In fact it reaches an extremely low level when we come to the following passage:—

label: text
text: They (the British residents) daunour for the right to have absolute sway over their workers and servants. What is life in a colony without the right of lord-hig it over a few slaves' Democracy? We have had enough of it at Home." But, of course, we need not dwell on this point, as we may be quite sure that it is the Governor's viewpoint that will prevail and not the "nobodies at Home, although lydees and gents in the Colony."

label: text
text: Naturally when a writer can find nothing better to inflict upon his readers than this sort of stuff, we expect a full repetition of the lie about the Shameen shooting affair, and we get it. "Massacres" is the term used, and while those guilty should be brought to justice, "assurances and guarantees should be given that such massacres will not be repeated in the future, etc." What does the "etcetera" stand for, we wonder? Perhaps that the British will also no longer consider themselves as being specially "ordained by Providence to preside over the destnies of various peoples. It is difficult to tell what is in the minds of these southern journalists.

text: MR. HO SAI-ON LAID TO REST.

label: text
text: The funeral of Mr. Ho Sai-on (seventh son of Mr. Ho Kom-tong), whose death has already been recorded in these columns, took place this morning from No. 29, Conduit Road, the 'cortege' with a large following, and headed by a band, arriving near the University ground at noon.

label: text
text: After a brief halt, during which the followers paid their last respects, the procession wended its way to the Chinese Cemetery.

label: text
text: The funeral was very largely attended by the deceased's relatives and prominent members of the Chinese community. Amongst the attendance were Messrs. Wong Kam-took, Ho Leung, Ho Kwong, Ho Wing, the Misses Ho Tung, the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotewall, Dr. Ma Chiu-ki, Messrs. M. K. and M. W. Lo, the Indian, Y.M.C.A. and Kowloon sections of the St. John Ambulance Brigade, Mr. E. Ralphs (Acting Commissioner), Mr. J. Ralston and Professor C. A. Middleton Smith.

label: text
text: The arrangements for the funeral were on a very elaborate scale.

text: A Briton, Frenchman, American, German, and a Chinese (said to be secretary to a Chinese General) have been arrested by the French Police for alleged arms smuggling.
